metadata.name: National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale
metadata.summary: Standardized 15-item bedside neurological examination quantifying acute stroke impairment.
clinical_pearls: Score what the patient actually does, not what you think they can do; never coach unless specified.
Do not go back and change earlier scores based on subsequent items.
Untestable (UN) items are excluded from the numeric sum and documented separately.
Objectively quantifies acute ischemic stroke severity; higher scores correlate with larger infarct volume on CT and MRI.

NIHSS scores obtained within the first 48 hours after stroke correlate with clinical outcomes at 3 months and 1 year (each 1-point increase lowers the odds of an excellent 3-month outcome by ~17% in TOAST).
Patients with a total score ≤ 4 generally have favorable outcomes and a high likelihood of functional independence regardless of treatment (~75% independent at 1 year).

Pitfall — High score & IV thrombolysis: Guidelines warn that IV tPA in patients with high NIHSS (> 22) carries increased risk of hemorrhagic conversion (17% ICH for NIHSS > 20 vs. 3% for < 10 in NINDS), though these patients also have the most severe baseline disability.
Pitfall — Posterior circulation blind spot: Even a large-territory posterior circulation stroke can present with a low or normal NIHSS score.

Pitfall — Interrater variability: Facial palsy, limb ataxia, neglect, level of consciousness, and dysarthria have lower interrater reliability and can be confounded by altered mental status; roughly 1 in 3 initial scores showed a clinically meaningful discrepancy between neurologists and emergency nurses (Comer et al., 2022).

Pitfall — Simplified alternative: The Modified NIHSS (mNIHSS) demonstrates higher interrater reliability with equivalent clinical performance, though it is less widely adopted than the original NIHSS.

interpretation.label: No Stroke Symptoms
interpretation.summary: Score 0: no measurable deficit on standard NIHSS items.
interpretation.clinical_note: Posterior circulation or isolated subtle deficits may still be present.

interpretation.label: Minor Stroke
interpretation.clinical_note: Assess whether deficits are disabling (e.g., aphasia, hemianopia, hand weakness) for reperfusion decisions.

interpretation.label: Moderate-to-Severe Stroke
interpretation.summary: Score 16–20: moderate-to-severe stroke; high likelihood of large vessel occlusion.

interpretation.label: Severe Stroke
interpretation.summary: Score 21–42: severe stroke with high morbidity and mortality risk.

assessment_guides.title: NIHSS Core Administration Rules & Coma Cascade
bedside_steps: Administer items strictly in order (1a through 11).
Record the patient's first effort; do not coach or allow repeated attempts except where specified (1b, 1c).
pitfalls_and_exceptions: Only use UN for amputation/joint fusion (items 5, 6, 7) or intubation/physical barrier (item 10).

assessment_guides.title: Item 1b: LOC Questions — Intubation & Language Rules
bedside_steps: Ask the patient for the current month and their age.
Only the initial answer counts; partial credit is not given for being close.
pitfalls_and_exceptions: Intubated patients, severe dysarthria, or non-aphasic language barriers who cannot speak are scored 1 (not 2).
Aphasic or stuporous patients who do not comprehend the questions are scored 2.

assessment_guides.title: Item 5a/5b: Motor Arm Technique & UN Criteria
bedside_steps: Extend arm 90° if sitting or 45° if supine, palms down, and release.
Count aloud from 1 to 10 seconds while watching for downward drift.
pitfalls_and_exceptions: Score 1 only if the arm drifts before 10 seconds without hitting the bed.
Score 2 if there is some effort against gravity but the arm hits the bed before 10 seconds.
Score UN ONLY for amputation or shoulder joint fusion (never for IV lines or weakness).

assessment_guides.title: Item 7: Limb Ataxia — Weakness Rule
bedside_steps: Test finger-nose-finger and heel-knee-shin bilaterally with eyes open.
pitfalls_and_exceptions: Score ataxia ONLY if present out of proportion to weakness.
In a paralyzed limb (score 4) or patient who cannot understand, score 0 (absent), NOT UN.

assessment_guides.title: Item 9: Best Language (Text Prompts)
bedside_steps: Assess comprehension and fluency throughout the exam, then ask the patient to read the standard sentences and name common bedside objects (e.g., watch, pen, chair, key, glove).
For intubated patients, assess written responses or comprehension.
exam_prompts: Read aloud: "I got home from work."
Read aloud: "Near the table in the dining room."
Read aloud: "They heard him speak on the radio last night."
pitfalls_and_exceptions: Score 3 only if mute/global aphasia with no usable speech or auditory comprehension.
Visual loss should not penalize item 9: place objects in the patient's hand to identify if blind.

assessment_guides.title: Item 10: Dysarthria (Standard Word List)
bedside_steps: Ask the patient to read or repeat the standard word list below without telling them why articulation is being tested.
exam_prompts: Words: MAMA · TIP-TOP · FIFTY-FIFTY · THANKS · HUCKLEBERRY · BASEBALL PLAYER
pitfalls_and_exceptions: Score UN ONLY if intubated or a physical barrier prevents speaking.
If severe aphasia prevents reading/repeating, assess clarity of any spontaneous speech; if mute, score 2.
